title: Who Gets Credit? How Audiences Judge Authorship in 1,214 Tool-Assisted Artworks
abstract: We showed 3,050 participants a set of 1,214 artworks made with varying degrees of generative assistance and asked them to judge authorship, skill and value. Disclosure of process, not the presence of AI, was the strongest predictor of how much credit audiences gave the artist. Works with a short, specific process note were rated as more skilful than both undisclosed AI-assisted works and fully manual works without notes.
source: Journal of Creative Computing 9(3) · Peer-reviewed · October 2026 · Lew, Menon & Brandvold, Studio for Creative Computing, Utrecht
author: Dr. Hanna Lew
cite: Lew, Menon & Brandvold (2026) · Journal of Creative Computing 9(3), 112–131
deck: A large study finds that how artists describe their process matters more to audiences than whether AI was involved at all.
disclosure: Statistical analysis in R. A language model was used to check this summary against the paper for accuracy; all text was written and approved by the authors.
findings: A specific process note raised perceived skill by 18% on average, compared with no note.
Vague labels such as "made with AI" lowered perceived authorship by 11%.
Practitioners in the sample judged human editing more generously than general audiences did.

blocks.text: Most debate about AI in art asks whether machine involvement should count against an artist. We wanted to measure something more practical: what audiences actually do with the information they are given, and whether artists can influence that through the way they describe their work.

We assembled 1,214 works from 212 consenting artists across illustration, painting, photography and print. Each work was tagged by stage of tool use: ideation, generation, editing, or none. Participants saw each work under one of four conditions: no information, a generic "made with AI" label, a specific process note written by the artist, or a note stating the work was fully manual.

Participants rated authorship, skill and how much they would pay for a print. We recruited 2,410 general-audience participants and 640 working practitioners, and preregistered our hypotheses before data collection.
Audiences are not asking whether a machine was involved. They are asking who made the decisions.

The practical lesson is that disclosure is not a penalty to be minimised. A two-sentence note naming the tool and the stage at which it was used, followed by what the artist did next, consistently earned more credit than silence. Generic labels did the opposite.

Ratings were collected online, on screens, and may not reflect how people respond to physical work in a gallery. Participants were drawn from eight countries, mostly in Europe and North America. We are now repeating the study with in-person audiences in Lagos, São Paulo and Seoul.
